data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference smuggles induction back in because the very act of preferring a corroborated theory for action implicitly assumes that the future will resemble the past, which is the definition of induction Popper sought to eliminate.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If Popper can define a non-probabilistic 'degree of corroboration' that justifies action without predicting the future, the charge fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference is purely aesthetic or psychological and not claimed as rational, the charge of 'smuggling' rational induction is misplaced.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'wager' is acknowledged as irrational but necessary, Popper admits the failure of pure critical rationalism.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"When a scientist chooses Theory A over Theory B because A has survived tests while B has not, they are effectively betting that A will continue to survive future tests. This bet requires a principle of the uniformity of nature or a belief that survival so far increases the likelihood of survival tomorrow. Without this hidden inductive premise, there is no rational basis within Popper's system to prefer A over B for practical action; both remain equally unproven and logically improbable.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
